title: Biomarker-guided post-transplant surveillance as a precision-medicine strategy in kidney transplantation
summary:
Kidney transplant patients with a high level of immune risk are more likely to experience rejection and poorer transplant outcomes. However, in current practice they are usually monitored in the same way as patients with low risk. This means that immune reactions against the transplanted kidney are often discovered only after some damage has already occurred.

New blood and urine tests can detect early signs of immune activity without the need for a biopsy. In this study, several modern biomarkers will be tested together — including donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA), immune markers in blood and urine, urinary chemokines, a virus that reflects immune strength (Torque Teno Virus, TTV), and molecular analyses of kidney biopsy tissue.

These tests will be used both in patients who are being routinely monitored after transplant (surveillance group) and in those who need a biopsy because of clinical changes such as higher creatinine or protein in the urine (for-cause group). This will help researchers understand how these biomarkers behave during early, silent immune activity as well as during visible kidney problems.

By comparing patients with different levels of immune risk, the study aims to find out whether a personalized monitoring strategy using these biomarkers can help detect rejection earlier and improve long-term kidney transplant success.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-Age ≥ 18 years
-Kidney transplant recipients (living or deceased donor) with a transplantation date after January 2026
-Kidney transplant recipients with a clinical indication for biopsy
-Written informed consent obtained after appropriate explanation of the study
-Willingness and ability to participate in all scheduled visits and examinations during the 36-month follow-up period (as part of routine care)
-Assignment to an immunological risk category (high, intermediate-high, intermediate-low, low) according to center practice
Exclusion criteria:
-Minors (<18 years)
-Refusal or inability to provide informed consent (e.g., cognitive impairment, language barrier without translation support)
-Participation in an interventional clinical study that influences immunological monitoring or therapy and could therefore bias the evaluation of study endpoints
-Other serious medical, psychological, or social reasons which, in the judgment of the investigators, make study participation unreasonable or infeasible
